1198.title: Humility of the fourth Guru
1198.hook: tradition says Guru Ram Das answered a visitor's question about his beard by wiping the visitor's feet
1198.howItsDone: Sikhs tell this story of Guru Ram Das and Baba Sri Chand when they speak of humility, and seva, humble service such as cleaning shoes and washing dishes at the gurdwara, is part of Sikh community life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the city he built: a pool, a bazaar and a sangat side by side in Ramdaspur. Your line was holy in the market.

Someone you respect comes to visit, a renunciant famous for his discipline. He looks you up and down and asks, with a small edge, why you've let your beard grow so long. A fair question, or a jab? There are easy answers: explain yourself, laugh it off, ask a question back. Why Sikhs keep their hair uncut came up earlier on this path; today's story is about the answer, not the hair. Sikh tradition tells it of Guru Ram Das, and his answer wasn't a word at all.
screen: `A RESPECTED VISITOR.` → `WHY SUCH A LONG BEARD?` → `THE ANSWER ISN'T A WORD.`

segments.voice: The visitor, tradition says, was Baba Sri Chand, the son of Guru Nanak, a respected ascetic in his own right, honored by the Udasi sadhus. He came to see the fourth Guru and asked about his long beard. Guru Ram Das answered: it's for wiping the feet of holy men like you. And then, the story goes, he knelt and began to do it. Three things make this land. First, he doesn't defend himself. A question with an edge invites an argument; he turns it into an invitation to serve. Second, he serves someone who might have been a rival. Here is the founder's own son, and the Guru now sitting in the founder's place kneels at his feet. The story is told with honor for both men. Third, the story matches his hymns. In a hymn that is part of the Rehras, the Sikh evening prayer, Guru Ram Das speaks to the Guru like this, paraphrased: we are like small worms and insects, O True Guru, and we seek your shelter; be kind, and light up the Name in us. That's not false modesty. It's a Guru who knows that the light he carries isn't his own. It sits close to the rest of his days: the Guru who asks for the dust of the Gursikh's feet, who builds a city around a pool for everyone, who answers a jab by kneeling. Humble service, in the stories about him, isn't thinking less of yourself. It's being free enough of yourself to kneel.

segments.voice: Look over today and find one job nobody wants, the dishes someone else left, shoes piled at the door, the trash nobody takes out. Picture yourself doing it slowly, without announcing it or keeping score, and let the breath settle on that picture, with Waheguru on each breath out if you pray.

1199.title: Guru Ram Das close
1199.hook: a routine, a city, and songs of longing: the fourth Guru's way
1199.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Guru Ram Das in the morning and evening prayers that include his hymns, at his gurpurab, and at the Harmandir Sahib in the city tradition says he began.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the humility of the fourth Guru: asked about his beard, he knelt to wipe a visitor's feet. Your line was humble service.

An alarm clock in the dark. A horse dressed for a wedding. A face you ache to see. A pool with a market at its edge. A man kneeling at a visitor's feet. Lay those on a table and they look like five different stories. They're all one Guru: Guru Ram Das, the fourth Guru, Mahala four. Today his section closes with one question: what holds those pieces together?
screen: `AN ALARM, A HORSE, A FACE.` → `A POOL, A MAN KNEELING.` → `ONE GURU.`

segments.voice: Three strands run through his days on this path. The first is a routine. His salok on the Gursikh gave a clock, not a definition: rise early, make the effort, bathe, remember the Name; then, sitting and standing, with breath and mouthful, keep remembering; then help someone else remember, and the Guru asks for your dust. A day with a shape. The second strand is a city. Tradition says he set a pool, a bazaar and a sangat side by side in Ramdaspur: the routine given a place to live, among other people, in the middle of buying and selling. The third strand is longing. The Ghorian, the horse songs, with the body as a gift that carries the soul home. The hymn of separation in Sri Rag: the ache, the friends you ask, the sight that heals it. And in the stories, the humility of a Guru who kneels. Here's how they fit. A routine without longing can harden into a chore, boxes ticked. Longing without a routine can drift, a beautiful ache that never gets out of bed. And both of them, without a city, stay private. Guru Ram Das holds all three together. The longing gives the routine its warmth. The routine gives the longing somewhere to go each morning. And the city, and the kneeling, keep both turned toward other people. Sikh tradition says he passed the Guruship to his son Arjan, who carries the Name into a new set of hymns. That's where the path goes next.
screen: `A ROUTINE: A DAY WITH A SHAPE.` · `A CITY: THE ROUTINE AMONG OTHERS.` · `LONGING: THE WARMTH INSIDE IT.` · `ALL THREE HELD TOGETHER.` · then, large: `THE FOURTH GURU'S WAY.`

segments.voice: Look back at the mornings since this stretch began, without grading them: did you rise a little earlier, even once, and what met you first? Then choose what tomorrow's first minutes will hold, and add one thing from these days, a breath for someone you miss, or thanks for the horse you ride. If you pray, Waheguru can open the morning.
Guru Ram Das close. A routine, a city, and songs of longing, held together by a Guru who kneels. Today's word.
Your line: the fourth guru's way. Longing gives the routine its warmth, and the routine gives longing a road. Until tomorrow.

1200.title: Fifty-two letters
1200.hook: Guru Arjan's long acrostic on the letters, a school for the soul (Gauri, ang 250)
1200.howItsDone: Sikhs read and study the Bavan Akhri in the Guru Granth Sahib, and its opening salok, on the Guru as mother and father, is recited and sung in Sikh prayer and kirtan.

segments.voice: Yesterday closed Guru Ram Das: a routine, a city, and songs of longing. Your line was the fourth guru's way.

A, apple. B, ball. C, cat. The alphabet chart on a classroom wall sticks a picture to each letter, and some of those pictures never quite come unstuck. Now aim that schoolroom trick somewhere else. Each letter opens a short lesson, not about apples or cats, but about the mind, the ego, death, grace, and the Name. That's what Guru Arjan, Guru Ram Das's son, did in a long hymn in Raga Gauri. Its name tells you what it is: Bavan Akhri.
screen: `A, APPLE. B, BALL.` → `EACH LETTER, A LESSON.` → `GURU ARJAN, IN GAURI.`

segments.voice: Bavan Akhri: fifty-two letters, the hymn's own title. It's an acrostic: stanza after stanza begins on a letter, and the letter becomes the doorway into a teaching. A school for the soul, with the alphabet as its timetable. But before the first letter there's a salok, and it tells you who the teacher is. Paraphrased: the Divine Guru is mother, the Divine Guru is father, the Divine Guru is master and the Transcendent Lord. The Guru is companion, the destroyer of ignorance, kin and brother. So this school begins with a relationship, not a lesson. The teacher is also a parent, a friend, the one who stays. Then the letters come. And this path has been circling letters a long time. In the first year we heard young Nanak asking his village teacher what the letters really pointed to. We heard the tradition of Guru Angad shaping the Gurmukhi letters so ordinary people could read the hymns. We heard the Japji say that through letters the Name is spoken and praise is sung. The Bavan Akhri stands in that line. Letters, for the Gurus, aren't only for contracts and shopping lists. They're a way to the Name, if you learn them for what they point to. That's the quiet point of an acrostic: letter after letter gets its turn, and each is taught to point the same way.
screen: `BAVAN AKHRI: FIFTY-TWO LETTERS.` · `FIRST, THE TEACHER: MOTHER, FATHER.` · `THE LETTERS AGAIN, ON THIS PATH.` · `THE WHOLE ALPHABET POINTS ONE WAY.` · then, large: `A SCHOOL FOR THE SOUL.`

segments.voice: Hold the first letter of your own name in your mind, the way a child traces it on a slate. Let it carry one lesson worth living by, patience if it's P, kindness if it's K, taking the first good one that comes rather than searching hard. If you pray, say Waheguru as you trace it.

1201.title: The Bavan Akhri's heart
1201.hook: cleverness without the Name goes nowhere, says one letter of the Bavan Akhri (Gauri, ang 260)
1201.howItsDone: Sikhs read the Bavan Akhri in the Guru Granth Sahib, and Sikh teachers turn to stanzas like this one when they speak of learning held with humility and pointed toward the Name.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Bavan Akhri, Guru Arjan's fifty-two letters: an acrostic where each letter opens a lesson, and the Guru is mother and father. Your line was the letters again.

Can a person know a great deal and still miss the point? Maybe you've met one: the uncle who can win any argument at the table and never seems happy, the friend who's read everything about love and can't keep a friendship going. Knowing isn't the problem. Something is missing from the middle of it. The Bavan Akhri hands that lesson to one letter of the alphabet.
screen: `KNOWING A GREAT DEAL.` → `STILL MISSING THE POINT.` → `ONE LETTER'S LESSON.`

segments.voice: The letter is sassa, the S sound in Gurmukhi. Its stanza, paraphrased: Sassa: give up your cleverness, you who don't understand. The Lord is not won over by clever tricks or by giving orders. You may try a thousand kinds of cleverness, but not one of them will go with you. Hear the play on the letter: sassa opens with siaanap, cleverness. The alphabet itself is teaching. A few days back, Guru Amar Das told the restless mind that no one finds the Lord through cleverness. Guru Arjan's stanza takes a different turn: it asks what your cleverness can carry with you. First, what the stanza doesn't say. It doesn't say learning is bad. This is a hymn built out of the alphabet. Guru Arjan isn't against letters, only a certain use of them. Second, the two things named: clever tricks and commands. Being smart enough to get your way, and powerful enough to order it. Both are ways of staying in control, and the Lord isn't won by either. Third, the thousand kinds. Multiply your cleverness as far as you like; not one goes with you. That's the stanza's measure: not how much you know, but what goes with you. In Sikh teaching, what goes with you is the Name. So learning is welcome, and letters are a gift. But learning without the Name at its center is like a beautifully built house with nobody living in it. What the Guru asks isn't less knowledge. It's knowledge with a heart: learned humbly, held loosely, pointed toward the Name.

segments.voice: Bring to mind something you're learning right now, a skill for work, a language, a recipe, a hymn, and ask it one quiet question: not what will you get me, but what are you for, who could you serve? Let an answer come, even a small one, and hold it for a few breaths, with Waheguru if you pray.
The Bavan Akhri's heart. Sassa's lesson: give up your cleverness; a thousand kinds of it won't go with you, but the Name will. Today's word.

1202.title: Bavan Akhri close
1202.hook: a long alphabet ending in grace
1202.howItsDone: The Bavan Akhri of Guru Arjan is part of the Guru Granth Sahib in Raga Gauri; some Sikhs read it through in their own study or hear it explained in katha at the gurdwara.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the heart of the Bavan Akhri: letters learned without the Name stay empty. Your line was learning with heart.

A school slate at the end of the day. Chalk dust in the corners, a row of letters copied over and over, a teacher's mark at the bottom. Guru Arjan's Bavan Akhri in Raga Gauri works like that slate, stretched across the Guru Granth Sahib from Ang two hundred fifty. Letter after letter, each one opens a lesson. Today, the bottom of the slate, where the teacher leaves the last mark. And the last mark isn't a grade. It's a gift.
screen: `A SLATE AT THE END OF THE DAY.` → `LETTER AFTER LETTER.` → `THE LAST MARK IS A GIFT.`

segments.voice: An acrostic sets up an expectation. Each letter is a step, and steps sound like effort: learn this, then this, and you'll arrive. The Bavan Akhri uses that shape, and along the way it says hard things, like the sassa stanza's warning about cleverness that goes nowhere. You'd expect the ending to reward the student who finished every letter. Instead, as this path reads it, a long alphabet ends in grace. The close turns from the student to the Giver: the Name comes through the Lord's mercy and the Guru's kindness, not through anyone's own cleverness. Sikh vocabulary has words for that turn. Kirpa is mercy, kindness given freely. Nadar is the gracious glance, the Lord looking with favor. Sikh teaching holds both together with effort. Sikhs are asked to rise, remember, work honestly, serve, and Gurbani speaks of the fruit of all that as a gift. Some readers hear the whole composition as a lesson in the right order of things. First you learn your letters. Then you find out who was holding the chalk. So the long schoolroom poem doesn't end by praising the pupil. It ends with the pupil looking up: the work was real, and the gift was bigger than the work.

1203.title: Salok Sehskriti
1203.hook: verses in a Sanskrit-flavored style, on the passing world (ang 1353)
1203.howItsDone: The Salok Sehskriti of Guru Nanak and Guru Arjan are part of the closing sections of the Guru Granth Sahib; they are read in full during an akhand path or sahaj path, and some Sikhs study them with a giani's help because of their unusual vocabulary.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Bavan Akhri closed: a long alphabet that ends in grace. Your line was ends in grace.

Some words wear a robe. Say thou instead of you, or hath instead of has, and the room changes: the sentence sounds older, like it came from a temple instead of a kitchen. Near the end of the Guru Granth Sahib, from Ang thirteen hundred fifty-three, sits a set of verses that does exactly that. They're called Salok Sehskriti, and their words wear the robe of an old learned language. Today, just listen to how it sounds.
screen: `SOME WORDS WEAR A ROBE.` → `ANG 1353.` → `A DIFFERENT SOUND.`

segments.voice: Sehskriti, sometimes spelled Sahaskriti, names the style. Call it Sanskrit-flavored; that's the plain way to say it. These are not verses in classical Sanskrit, but speech dressed in its endings and its weight. Lines close on sounds like ang and ah, so the ear hears something stately and old. Guru Nanak's saloks open the set, and Guru Arjan's verses follow. Here's the surprise. Sanskrit was the language of learned pandits and temple scholarship. On the pages around these verses, the Gurus sing in the speech of ordinary people. Here they pick up the learned register instead. Why? The text doesn't explain itself. Some readers suggest it speaks to the learned in their own manner. Others hear it simply as range: the Guru can sing in the village voice and the scholar's voice, and say the same truth in both. And what the verses say in that robe isn't new. Paraphrased, they keep turning to how quickly this world passes, and how only remembering the Lord stays. Grand dress, and the message Sikhs hear all through the Granth. A learned language doesn't make the Name truer, and a plain one doesn't make it smaller. The Guru wears whichever robe reaches the listener.

segments.voice: If you can find the Salok Sehskriti, from Ang thirteen hundred fifty-three, read two of them aloud, slowly, in Gurmukhi or transliteration, and listen to the endings and the weight of the sound rather than chasing every word. If you can't find them, listen to the plainest sound near you, a fan, a bird, traffic, and notice that it, too, is a voice. Then let the sound fade into the breath.
Salok Sehskriti. Verses near the end of the Guru Granth Sahib in a Sanskrit-flavored style, speaking of the passing world. Today's word.
Your line: the old tongue. Under the robe, the same body. That's today, done.

1204.title: The Sehskriti's warnings
1204.hook: wealth, youth and family are passing, it says (Salok Sehskriti)
1204.howItsDone: Guru Arjan's Salok Sehskriti are read during a full reading of the Guru Granth Sahib, and lines like these are often explained in katha, where gianis set the warnings about passing things beside the Sikh honor for family life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Salok Sehskriti and their stately sound. Your line was the old tongue.

Katanch. Katanch. Katanch. The word knocks like a hand on a door, again and again. It opens one of Guru Arjan's verses in the Salok Sehskriti, and roughly it asks: where is? who is? Where is the mother, where is the father, where is the wife, the son? A question asked that many times in a row stops being a question and becomes a drumbeat. Yesterday was the old style. Today is what that style says, and it's a plain warning.
screen: `KATANCH, KATANCH, KATANCH.` → `WHERE IS? WHO IS?` → `A QUESTION BECOMES A DRUMBEAT.`

segments.voice: Here's the verse, paraphrased. Who is mother, who is father, who is wife, who are the children you delight in? Who are brother, friend and kin, and what is the pull of the household? The bright, enchanting beauty of the world: you see it, and it leaves. What stays with you, Nanak says, is the remembrance of the Lord. Put simply, these warnings name three things that pass: wealth, youth, family. Now a careful note, because this is easy to mishear. Sikh teachers don't read it as a command to walk away from family. This path has seen Guru Ram Das build a town and pass the Guruship to his son, and Sikh teaching honors the householder's life. Katanch isn't asking whether your mother matters. It's asking where she can go with you, in the end, and where you can go with her. The honest answer: not all the way. Every bond has a door it can't pass through. Some readers hear the verse less as a loss and more as a sorting. Love your people fully, it seems to say, and don't make them carry the weight only the Name can hold. If a loss is heavy on you right now, you don't have to carry it alone: in the US, call or text 988, or reach local emergency help.
screen: `WHO IS MOTHER, WHO IS FATHER?` · `NOT A COMMAND TO LEAVE HOME.` · `EVERY BOND HAS A DOOR.` · `ONLY THE NAME GOES ALL THE WAY.` · then, large: `PASSING THINGS.`

segments.voice: Choose something you love that won't last forever: a cup you use every morning, a season, your own strength. Hold it in your mind, or in your hands if it's near, and loosen your grip a little, the way you'd hold a bird. Be grateful it's here and honest that it passes, and if you pray, let Waheguru ride each breath out.
The Sehskriti's warnings. Mother, father, child, the world's bright beauty: they pass, this verse says; the remembrance of the Lord stays. Today's word.
Your line: passing things. That closes a week of letters and old tongues. Until tomorrow.
